title: Linear Search
prompt: Write linear_search(arr, target). Scan the array left to right, one element at a time, and return the index of the first match, or -1 if target never appears. arr is NOT assumed to be sorted.
method_note: Method check: on a 200-item 'not found' case, a real left-to-right scan takes roughly n steps. Finishing suspiciously fast (e.g. a hidden binary search, or Python's `in`) is rejected even if the answer is right.

title: Binary Search
prompt: Write binary_search(arr, target). arr is sorted ascending. Repeatedly look at the middle of the remaining range and eliminate half the search space each step, until you find target or run out of range. Return the index, or -1.
method_note: Method check: real binary search on 1000 items takes roughly log2(1000) ~ 10 steps. Anywhere near 1000 steps means it's secretly a linear scan wearing a binary-search name.

title: Bubble Sort
prompt: Write bubble_sort(arr) returning a NEW list sorted ascending. Repeatedly sweep through the list comparing neighbouring pairs and swapping if out of order, until a full sweep makes no swaps. No sorted()/.sort() shortcuts.
method_note: Method check: on a 30-item reverse-sorted worst case, a real compare-and-swap sort does on the order of n^2 work. A sorted() call finishes in ~1 step and is rejected -- the output is right, the method isn't.

title: Selection Sort
prompt: Write selection_sort(arr) returning a NEW list sorted ascending. For each position, scan the remaining unsorted part for the minimum, then swap it into place. No sorted()/.sort() shortcuts.
method_note: Method check: same idea as bubble sort -- real selection sort does O(n^2) work on a 25-item worst case; sorted()/.sort() shortcuts finish almost instantly and are rejected.

title: Insertion Sort
prompt: Write insertion_sort(arr) returning a NEW list sorted ascending. Build up the sorted section one element at a time: take the next element and shift it backwards through the sorted section until it's in the right place. No sorted()/.sort() shortcuts.
method_note: Method check: reverse-sorted input is insertion sort's worst case -- every new element has to shift all the way to the front, so a real implementation does on the order of n^2 work. sorted()/.sort() shortcuts finish almost instantly and are rejected.

title: Purpose of Big O
prompt: What does Big O notation describe about an algorithm?
choices: The exact number of seconds it takes to run
How its worst-case running time/work grows as the input size grows
How many lines of code it has
The programming language it was written in
explanation: Big O describes the growth rate of an algorithm's time (or space) requirement as the input size n increases -- not a literal stopwatch time.

title: Big O of Binary Search
prompt: What is the worst-case Big O time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
explanation: Binary search halves the remaining search space every step, so the number of steps grows logarithmically with n.

title: Big O of Bubble Sort
prompt: What is the worst-case Big O time complexity of bubble sort?
explanation: Bubble sort compares/swaps neighbouring pairs across repeated full passes, giving roughly n^2 comparisons in the worst case (reverse-sorted input).

title: Big O of Linear Search
prompt: What is the worst-case Big O time complexity of linear search?
explanation: In the worst case (target absent, or at the very end) a linear search has to check every one of the n elements.

title: Recursive Factorial

method_note: Method check: this counts self-calls. A correct recursive solution calls itself about n times; a for/while-loop version calls itself once and is rejected, even with the right return value.

title: Gantt Charts
prompt: In the 'investigate' phase of the development framework, what is a Gantt chart used for?
choices: Testing the final solution against user requirements
Scheduling tasks over time to plan and track a development project
Storing data in a relational structure
explanation: A Gantt chart is a project-scheduling tool that lays out tasks and their timeframes, used when planning a development schedule.

title: Linear vs Iterative Development
prompt: What's the key difference between a linear and an iterative development process?
choices: Linear repeats every phase in cycles; iterative only runs once
Linear moves through phases once in sequence; iterative repeats/refines phases based on feedback
Linear is only for databases; iterative is only for networks
explanation: A linear process moves straight through investigate -> design -> develop -> evaluate once. An iterative process cycles back through earlier phases as the solution is refined.

title: Purpose of a Stub
prompt: Why would a programmer write a 'stub' function while developing a larger program?
choices: To permanently replace a function that isn't needed
To act as a placeholder for an unfinished module so the rest of the program can be built and tested around it
explanation: A stub is a minimal, temporary placeholder implementation (e.g. returning a fixed value) that lets the rest of the program be structured, run and tested before every module is finished.

title: Clear Mainline
prompt: Why is 'a clear, uncluttered mainline with one logical task per subroutine' considered good practice?
choices: It makes the program run faster on any hardware
It makes the overall program easier to read, test and maintain by breaking it into understandable, focused pieces
It is required by every programming language's syntax
It removes the need for any comments
explanation: Splitting a program into small, single-purpose subroutines with a clean top-level mainline improves readability, testability and long-term maintainability -- it isn't about raw speed.

title: Version Control
prompt: What problem does version control (e.g. Git) primarily solve during software development?
choices: It prevents all runtime errors automatically
It tracks changes to code over time, letting developers collaborate and revert to earlier versions if something breaks
It replaces the need for testing
explanation: Version control systems track the history of changes to a codebase, support collaboration between developers, and allow reverting to a previous working version.

title: Regular Backups
prompt: Why does good programming practice recommend regular backups of code and data?
choices: To make the program run faster
To protect against loss from hardware failure, accidental deletion or corruption
Backups are only needed for network communications, not programming
explanation: Regular backups protect the project against data loss from things like disk failure, accidental deletion, or corrupted files.

title: Purpose of Unit Testing
prompt: What is the main purpose of unit testing?
choices: Checking that the whole finished system meets user requirements
Checking that an individual function/module performs correctly in isolation
Measuring how many users the system can support
Reviewing the ethical implications of a system
explanation: Unit tests target one small piece of code (a function or module) in isolation to confirm it behaves correctly before it's combined with everything else.

title: Acceptance vs Unit Testing
prompt: How does acceptance testing differ from unit testing?
choices: Acceptance testing checks individual functions; unit testing checks the whole system
Acceptance testing checks whether the finished solution meets the user's functional requirements; unit testing checks individual pieces of code
They are two names for the same process
Acceptance testing is only done by the original developer
explanation: Acceptance testing is a user-focused check that the overall solution does what was asked for, while unit testing verifies individual code units work correctly.

title: Live Test Data
prompt: Why would a tester use 'live' test data (large file sizes, a realistic mix of transaction types, real response times, high data volumes) instead of just a couple of made-up examples?
choices: Live data is easier to type in manually
It makes sure testing reflects how the system will actually behave under real operating conditions, including performance under load
It removes the need for any other kind of testing
Live data guarantees there will be no bugs
explanation: Live/realistic test data (volume, mixed transaction types, timing) helps reveal problems -- like performance or load issues -- that small, tidy sample data would never expose.

title: Actual vs Expected Output
prompt: During testing, what does 'comparing actual output with expected output' mean?
choices: Running the program twice and comparing the running time
Checking whether the result the program produced for a test case matches the result you calculated it SHOULD produce
Comparing your code style with another programmer's
Checking whether the code compiles without errors
explanation: For each test case you predict/calculate the expected result ahead of time, then compare it against what the program actually returns -- a mismatch flags a bug.

title: Load Testing
prompt: What does 'load testing' (testing with a high volume of data) specifically check?
choices: Whether the program's variable names follow conventions
How the system performs -- speed, stability, resource use -- when handling a large volume of data or many transactions at once
Whether the program has any syntax errors
Whether the developer documented their code
explanation: Load testing pushes a system with a realistic (large) volume of data or traffic to see whether performance holds up, rather than just checking correctness on small inputs.

title: Fix: Count Negatives

title: Types of Errors
prompt: A program crashes partway through execution because it tries to divide a number by zero. What TYPE of error is this?
explanation: A runtime error only shows up while the program is actually running (e.g. division by zero, index out of range) -- the code is syntactically valid and will happily compile.

title: Syntax vs Logic Errors
prompt: A program runs without crashing but consistently produces the wrong answer (e.g. it used '<' where it should have used '<='). What TYPE of error is this?
explanation: A logic error is code that's valid and runs fine, but doesn't do what the programmer intended -- the program logic itself is flawed.

title: Breakpoints
prompt: What does setting a breakpoint while debugging let a programmer do?
choices: Permanently delete a line of code
Pause execution at that line so the current variable values can be inspected
explanation: A breakpoint pauses execution at a chosen line so the developer can inspect variable values and step through the program to find where behaviour goes wrong.

title: Desk Checking
prompt: What is 'desk checking' (using a trace table)?
choices: Automated testing performed by the compiler
Manually walking through code line by line on paper, tracking variable values, to find where the logic goes wrong
Checking the physical desk setup of a workstation
A way to measure a network's bandwidth
explanation: Desk checking means tracing through the code by hand (often with a trace table of variable values) to find logic errors without running the program.

title: Index Out of Range
prompt: An array has 5 elements (valid indices 0 to 4). Which of these causes an 'index out of range' runtime error?
explanation: Valid indices for a 5-element array run from 0 to 4 -- index 5 is one past the end and triggers an index-out-of-range error.

title: Encapsulation
prompt: What does 'encapsulation' mean in object-oriented programming?
choices: A class having many unrelated responsibilities
Bundling data (attributes) and the behaviour (methods) that operates on it together inside one object, controlling access to its internals
Making one class inherit from many other classes at once
explanation: Encapsulation bundles an object's data and the methods that work on it together, typically hiding/protecting internal details from the outside.

title: Abstraction
prompt: What does 'abstraction' mean in object-oriented programming?
choices: Exposing every internal implementation detail of a class
Hiding complex implementation details behind a simple, well-defined interface the user of the class interacts with
Making a class impossible to instantiate
explanation: Abstraction means presenting a simple interface (e.g. deposit()/withdraw()) while hiding the complicated details of how it's implemented underneath.

title: Polymorphism
prompt: In the Animal/Dog example, calling .speak() gives a different result depending on whether the object is an Animal or a Dog. What OOP concept does this demonstrate?
explanation: Polymorphism lets objects of different (related) classes respond to the same method call in their own way -- here, speak() behaves differently for Animal vs Dog.

title: Why Use Inheritance
prompt: What is the main benefit of using inheritance (e.g. Dog extends Animal) instead of writing Dog as a completely separate, unrelated class?
choices: It makes the program run in less memory automatically
It lets Dog reuse Animal's existing attributes/methods and only add or override what's different, avoiding duplicated code
It is required by Python syntax for every class
It prevents the class from ever being instantiated
explanation: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse a parent class's code and only define what's new or different, reducing duplication and modelling an 'is-a' relationship.

title: Variable vs Constant

explanation: A constant models fixed data that should not be reassigned.
